clinicalPearls: A subacute encephalitis caused by persistent measles virus infection of the brain occurring specifically in immunocompromised patients
It is seen in children and adults with impaired cell-mediated immunity, such as leukaemia and lymphoma, chemotherapy, HIV, or transplantation
Unlike SSPE, the latent interval is short, typically weeks to a few months after measles exposure or infection, and the illness may lack a preceding rash
Presentation is with altered mental status, focal neurological deficits, and, very characteristically, refractory focal seizures including epilepsia partialis continua
Because antibody responses are blunted by immunosuppression, cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody may be low or absent, unlike the high titres of SSPE
Diagnosis rests on detecting measles virus RNA or antigen and viral inclusions in brain tissue, supported by imaging, since serology is unreliable in these hosts
The prognosis is poor; there is no established effective therapy, and prevention through avoiding measles exposure and ensuring immunity in contacts is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Measles inclusion body encephalitis develops when the measles virus persists and replicates within the central nervous system of a host whose cell-mediated immunity is too impaired to clear it. In contrast to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, where a defective virus smoulders for years and provokes intense antibody production, here the immunosuppressed brain permits relatively active viral replication over a much shorter period with only a weak immune response. Neurones and glia contain intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies packed with viral nucleocapsids, and there is neuronal loss with comparatively little inflammatory infiltrate because the immune response is suppressed. The rapidly progressive cortical involvement produces the characteristic intractable focal seizures and focal deficits, and the blunted humoral response explains why CSF measles antibody is often unhelpful for diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex and other viral encephalitides in the immunocompromised
additionalInvestigations: Detection of measles virus RNA by PCR or antigen in cerebrospinal fluid or brain tissue
Brain biopsy showing intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies with immunostaining for measles antigen
MRI of the brain to identify cortical and subcortical signal change
Electroencephalography, often showing focal epileptiform activity rather than the periodic complexes of SSPE
Assessment of immune status including HIV testing, CD4 count, and chemotherapy or transplant history
Measles exposure and immunisation history of the patient and close contacts
redFlags: Refractory focal seizures or epilepsia partialis continua in an immunocompromised patient
Progressive decline in conscious level or new focal deficits
Recent measles exposure or infection in a severely immunosuppressed host
Status epilepticus or rapid neurological deterioration
reference.prognosis: The outlook is poor, with most patients deteriorating over weeks to months and high mortality; survival and any recovery depend heavily on restoring immune function, and no antiviral regimen is reliably effective.
pitfalls: Excluding measles because CSF antibody is low, when the immunosuppressed host cannot mount a strong response
Confusing MIBE with SSPE despite their different time course, immune context, and EEG findings
Failing to obtain brain tissue or molecular testing when serology is unrevealing
Overlooking measles exposure in an immunocompromised patient with new refractory seizures
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Restore cell-mediated immunity where possible by reducing immunosuppression, treating HIV with antiretroviral therapy, or achieving immune reconstitution
Attempt antiviral therapy with ribavirin (systemic and/or intraventricular), with or without interferon, recognising the limited anecdotal evidence
Aggressive control of refractory focal seizures and epilepsia partialis continua with combination antiepileptic drugs
Neurocritical supportive care addressing airway protection, nutrition and raised intracranial pressure
Multidisciplinary input from neurology, infectious diseases and the primary immunosuppressing service
Early discussion of the grave prognosis with palliative and family support where deterioration is relentless
Prevention through measles immunisation of susceptible contacts and immunoglobulin prophylaxis after exposure in immunocompromised patients
